newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian budget may include corporate tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian budget may include corporate tax cut.

text.p: Malaysia's 1997 budget may contain a one to two percentage point cut in the 30 percent corporate tax in a bid to stay competitive with neighbouring countries, economists said on Tuesday.

"If you were a multinational corporation and looking where to go, Malaysia is a good bet, but if you want to give a profit incentive, the corporate taxes are the way to go," said Rajeev Malik, an economist with Jardine Fleming.
The budget is expected to be unveiled next Friday, and securities research firms have been busy publishing reports outlining their best guesses for what it contains.
Jupiter Securities said it sees corporate tax cuts "by at least one percent". In a report on Tuesday, it said: "Corporate rates may be lowered to be competitive regionally."
A tax rate of 29 or 28 percent for companies in Malaysia would still put it above Singapore, where taxes were trimmed from 27 to 26 percent this year and could ease to 25 percent.
Thailand is contemplating a reduction to 27 from 30 percent to boost economic growth, an economist with a local research house noted. "I think Malaysia will be under competitive pressure," he said.
Malaysia last reduced corporate taxes in the 1995 budget, when it moved rates down to 30 from 32 percent.
"We would not be surprised if the government decides to cut the corporate income tax rate by one or two percentage points again this year," said a report by Capitalcorp Securities.
But, the firm added: "The likelihood is rather slim in view that the last concession was only recently."
Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said in September the government was considering incentives and tax reductions to increase competitiveness.
"I would personally favour tax reductions, which have been the government's policy in the last few years," Anwar said.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Monday the budget would focus on reducing unnecessary imports to narrow the country's balance-of-payments deficit.

Malaysia reported a current-account deficit of 17.8 billion ringgit last year and has forecast the gap will narrow to 17 billion this year. But economists project the current-account gap could drop to around 14 billion ringgit this year.
